citations.quote: Data architects create and maintain organizational knowledge about data and the systems through which it moves.
These data flows map the movement of data to business processes, locations, business roles, and to technical components.
both need to be reflected in current state and target state (architecture perspective), and also in transition state (project perspective)
Models in each level map to models in other levels. Model lineage is created using these maps.
Data flows are a type of data lineage documentation that depicts how data moves through business processes and systems.
Uncontrolled data delivery, data copies, and interface 'spaghetti' relationships make organizations less efficient and reduce trust in the data.
Determining data lineage impact : Ensures that business rules in the applications along the data flow are consistent and traceable.
Replication is a common way to improve application performance and make data more readily available, but it can also create inconsistencies in the data.
Identify these documents and evaluate them for accuracy, completeness, and level of detail.
Most business capabilities require data as an input; others also produce data on which other business capabilities are dependent.
Product Management and Customer Management do not depend on anything else and thus constitute Master Data.
Enforce the use of system of record or other authoritative data.
Because they compile an inventory of IT assets, such tools collect and contain valuable Metadata about systems and the data they contain.
Architecture designs can be aspirational or future-looking, implemented and active, or plans for retirement. What they represent should be clearly documented.
Current : Products currently supported and used Deployment period : Products deployed for use in the next 1-2 years
Retirement : Products the organization has retired or intends to retire within a year
Typically, the Enterprise Data Architecture starts with Master Data areas that are in great need for improvements
both a data architect and a Data Steward should be assigned to each subject area and even to each entity within a subject area
the business meaning of the data, the business rules for transforming the data, and the operational history and lineage of the data
Data Integration and Interoperability is critical to Data Warehousing and Business Intelligence, as well as Reference Data and Master Data Management
Semantic conversion : Conversion of data values to maintain consistent semantic representation.
targets to be loaded, rules for identifying target rows for update (if any), and any transformation rules or calculations to be applied
State information and process dependencies must be monitored by the target application load process.
For example, process Master Data or dimensional data prior to transactional data that uses that Master Data.
The use of multiple interfaces to obtain data will lead to inconsistencies in the data sent to downstream systems.
Data Warehouses, Data Marts, Operational Data Stores, and Master Data Management hubs are the most well-known examples of data hubs.
Process Controls are the components that ensure shipment, delivery, extraction, and loading of data is accurate and complete.
A common example includes information on the securities sold through a stock exchange and associated prices (current and historical).
the 'service' concept is also used within an organization to provide enterprise data or data services to various functions and operational systems
having an agreed upon exchange format or data layout between systems can significantly simplify data interoperability in an enterprise
high-level data lineage: how the data under analysis is acquired or created by the organization, where it moves and is changed within the organization
Detailed lineage can include the rules according to which data is changed, and the frequency of changes.
legacy data manipulation objects should be documented to ensure that the organization can analyze the impact of any changes in the data flow
Actual data structure and contents always differ from what is assumed.
Assessing accuracy requires comparing to a definitive set of data that has been determined to be correct.
The requirement to profile data must be balanced with an organization's security and privacy regulations.
Business rules fall into one of four categories: definitions of business terms, facts relating terms to each other, constraints or action assertions, and derivations.
For Master Data Management, business rules include match rules, merge rules, survivorship rules, and trust rules.
The business analyst or data steward can extract the rules from existing documentation (like use cases, specifications, or system code)
Mapping sources to targets involves specifying the rules for transforming data from one location and format to another.
Include business definitions and technical definitions (structure, format, size), as well as the transformation of data between the persistent data stores.
Review all data transformation mapping design and changes with by business subject matter experts in each involved system.
a purely technical approach to DII can lead to errors in the data mappings and transformations
Business stakeholders should approve changes to any of these business rules.
One approach is to determine what events trigger governance reviews (exceptions or critical events).
such as mandated reviews of models, auditing of Metadata, gating of deliverables, and required approvals for changes to transformation rules
Prior to the development of interfaces or the provision of data electronically, develop a data sharing agreement or memorandum of understanding (MOU)
acceptable use of data to be exchanged, approved by the business data stewards of the data in question
The data sharing agreements should specify anticipated use and access to the data, restrictions on use, as well as expected service levels
Governance is required to ensure that knowledge of data origins and movement is documented.
limitations to the uses of data and in order to abide by these, it is necessary to know where data moves and persists
that require organizations be able to describe where their data originated and how it has been changed as it has moved through various systems
Forward and backward data lineage (i.e., where did data get used and where did it come from) is critical as part of the impact analysis

rows.dmbok_position: The DMBOK2 describes lineage as documentation of how data is acquired or created and where it moves and changes, adds that detailed lineage records the change rules and their frequency, treats data flows as a form of lineage documentation, and says custom ETL and legacy data-manipulation objects should be documented so the impact of flow changes can be analysed. It calls forward and backward lineage critical to impact analysis, lists determining lineage impact among data-architecture activities that keep business rules along a flow consistent and traceable, makes governance responsible for keeping knowledge of data origins and movement documented, and notes that emerging compliance standards expect organisations to explain where data originated and how it changed.
caveats: 'Lineage completeness' has no counterpart term in the DMBOK2 text read, and no completeness measure is defined there; alignment is judged on documented lineage and impact analysis, not on the term.
Chapter 12 (Metadata) is the DMBOK2's main treatment of lineage as metadata and lies outside this unit (read in unit 5); this row rests on Chapters 4 and 8 only.
rows.status_rationale: ARCHITECTURE.md gives the Mapping & Lineage Agent source-target mapping analysis, lineage completeness, dependency mapping and downstream impact, and HANDOFF.md's success criteria require lineage to be linkable to downstream impact; together these cover the lineage-documentation and impact-analysis activities the DMBOK2 describes. The gap is wording only: the project names the downstream direction, while the DMBOK2 pairs forward and backward lineage and separates high-level from detailed lineage, which the project text leaves implicit. Proposed wording (for human approval): name both forward and backward lineage and say whether high-level or detailed lineage is expected.

rows.dmbok_position: The DMBOK2 describes mapping as specifying the rules for transforming data from one location and format to another, covering targets, update rules and any transformation rules or calculations, and names semantic conversion as a transformation whose purpose is to keep the meaning of data values consistent. It treats these rules as a business matter: metadata is expected to track business meaning, transformation rules and lineage together and to record business as well as technical definitions of the data and its transformation, business stakeholders should approve changes to the rules, mapping designs and changes should be reviewed with business subject matter experts in each involved system, and a purely technical approach is said to invite errors in mappings and transformations; separately, models are mapped across levels of the enterprise data model, which creates model lineage.
caveats: The DMBOK2 text read gives no test for whether meaning has been preserved; 'did the meaning survive the transformation' is the project's framing, which the semantic conversion example supports only in spirit.

HANDOFF.md's human-approval list does not name changes to mapping or transformation rules explicitly (production changes and governance decisions cover them by implication), whereas the DMBOK2 places approval of such changes with business stakeholders.
rows.status_rationale: The Mapping & Lineage Agent's key question in ARCHITECTURE.md ('Did the meaning survive the transformation?'), together with its source-target mapping analysis, transformation identification and mapping-definition consistency responsibilities, is the concern the DMBOK2 addresses through semantic conversion and business review of mappings; HANDOFF.md's success criterion that mappings can be linked back to meaning is in the same spirit as the DMBOK2's cross-level model mapping. The project leaves mapping-specification contents and the approver of mapping-rule changes to the organisation's own process, and HANDOFF.md reserves production changes and governance decisions to humans, which is consistent with the DMBOK2 placing approval with business stakeholders. Proposed citation (general industry context): reference the semantic conversion and mapping-review passages where the key question is stated.

dmbok_terms: Chain of dependencies between business capabilities
rows.dmbok_position: The DMBOK2 does not use the term data contract; its nearest constructs are the data sharing agreement or memorandum of understanding, to be agreed before interfaces are built, approved by the business data stewards of the data and specifying anticipated use, access, restrictions and expected service levels, and an agreed exchange format or data layout between systems. It treats dependencies as business capabilities that need data other capabilities produce, as process dependencies that the target load process must monitor, and as lineage knowledge that sharing agreements rely on to know where data moves and persists.
caveats: 'Data contract' and 'upstream dependency management' are not DMBOK2 terms in the text read; treating the data sharing agreement and the data exchange specification as the closest constructs is the reader's interpretation and needs human confirmation.
The DMBOK2 handles dependencies as architecture, integration and lineage-impact concerns rather than as a named stewardship activity, so no single passage matches 'upstream dependency management'.
rows.status_rationale: README.md lists data contracts and upstream dependency management as stewardship responsibilities; ARCHITECTURE.md names data-contracts/ only as a possible Stewardship-as-Code directory and gives the Mapping & Lineage Agent dependency mapping (and the Exception & Root-Cause Agent 'identify common upstream dependencies'); BUILD-BACKLOG.md lists 'data contract generation' as future work; AGENT-CONTRACT-TEMPLATE.md lets an agent treat an 'approved data contract' as authoritative. No repository artefact says what a data contract contains or who approves it, and 'upstream dependency management' is not a defined activity, so the concept is present but under-specified and uses a term the DMBOK2 does not, whereas the DMBOK2 data sharing agreement has stated contents and business data steward approval. Proposed wording (for human approval): note that 'data contract' corresponds to what the DMBOK2 calls a data sharing agreement plus exchange specification (general industry context), and use the DMBOK2 contents as a checklist when the data-contracts/ artefact is first designed.

dmbok_terms: Match, merge, survivorship and trust rules
rows.dmbok_position: In Chapters 4 and 8 the DMBOK2 does not describe reference or master data stewardship itself (Chapter 10 does, and is read in unit 4); it treats master data as a first-order architecture and integration concern: capabilities that depend on nothing else constitute master data, enterprise data architecture typically starts with master data areas, integration is described as critical to reference data and master data management, and master data is to be processed before the transactional data that uses it. It names master data management hubs as a kind of data hub, lists match, merge, survivorship and trust rules as the business rules specific to master data management, and says a business analyst or data steward can extract business rules from existing documentation or system code.
caveats: Chapter 10 (Reference and Master Data) is outside this unit; the passages cited treat master and reference data as inputs to architecture and integration design and do not describe stewardship duties for them, so the status and options are provisional pending unit 4.

The master data example in the roadmap discussion rests partly on Figure 27 (missing from the converted text); only the one prose sentence quoted is relied on, and the example itself is unverifiable from text.
rows.status_rationale: ARCHITECTURE.md lists trading, orders, executions, transactions, positions, TBOR, IBOR, ABOR, valuation, NAV, reconciliation, regulatory reporting, enterprise data products and relevant source platforms as possible Context Agent content areas, and no project design, contract, schema or evaluation file mentions reference data or master data. The DMBOK2 treats both as managed parts of data management that architecture and integration must serve, so the absence of any stewardship artefact is a gap rather than an alignment. The status is provisional until merged with unit 4, which reads the DMBOK2's own reference and master data chapter.
proposal_options: Name reference data and master data as explicit content areas of the Investment Operations Context Agent, with no new agent or artefact type, in line with the DMBOK2 view that architecture typically starts with master data areas [DMBOK2-C04-17] and that integration is critical to reference and master data management [DMBOK2-C08-02]; this is the cheapest change but gives stewards context about the data, not stewardship of it.

Add a reference-and-master-data register as a Stewardship-as-Code artefact that names each data hub and the match, merge, survivorship and trust rules governing it, using the DMBOK2 hub and master data rule vocabulary [DMBOK2-C08-08] [DMBOK2-C08-20]; this brings the data itself under steward review and human approval but needs an owner and upkeep that the project has not assigned.

rows.dmbok_position: The DMBOK2 text read says only that, when data is reused, the system of record or other authoritative data should be enforced, and that accuracy can be assessed only against a definitive set of data already determined to be correct. It also asks that existing system documentation be evaluated for accuracy and completeness and observes that real data always differs from what is assumed; it offers information on securities and their prices as a common example of data-as-a-service, but says nothing on how an AI assistant should rank internal documentation against general knowledge.
caveats: The DMBOK2 text read mentions 'system of record' once, in the project-reuse guidance; it does not address which sources an AI assistant may treat as authoritative, so the rule that the internal documented position outranks general knowledge is project-specific.

In the repository 'system of record' appears only in the open question on where Orchestrator case state is held (docs/ARCHITECTURE-RISKS.md Open Question 4; docs/IMPLEMENTATION-SEQUENCE.md), not for investment data.

Whether externally supplied securities and price data counts as an authoritative source is a project decision; the data-as-a-service passage is only an example of such data, not a statement about authority.
rows.status_rationale: The principle that authoritative sources outrank general knowledge is present in README.md (principle 3), in ARCHITECTURE.md's INTERNAL DOCUMENTED POSITION label, in the Authoritative Sources section required by AGENT-CONTRACT-TEMPLATE.md and in the internal-only authoritative_sources list of contracts/definition-and-cde-agent.contract.json, and it fits the DMBOK2 preference for authoritative data. It differs in object and term: the project ranks approved documents and registers as evidence for agents (the contract's glossary/catalog system and CDE-criteria repositories are still unidentified), uses 'system of record' only for the Orchestrator's case-state store, and names no system of record for investment data, whereas the DMBOK2 phrase concerns the authoritative source of the data itself; the ranking of internal over general knowledge has no DMBOK2 counterpart. Proposed wording (for human approval): distinguish 'authoritative source' (an approved document or register an agent may rely on) from 'system of record' (the system holding the authoritative copy of a data domain) in AGENT-CONTRACT-TEMPLATE.md and the Context Agent's content-area list, and keep the internal-over-general ranking as a project rule.

rows.dmbok_position: The DMBOK2 says data architects create and maintain organisational knowledge about data and the systems it moves through, held in artefacts such as data flow design (which maps data movement to business processes, locations, roles and technical components) and in asset-inventory metadata about systems, and says existing system documentation should be evaluated for accuracy, completeness and level of detail. It also asks that architecture designs be documented as aspirational, implemented or planned for retirement, shows specifications in current, target and transition state, and describes enterprise data or data services offered inside an organisation to functions and operational systems.
caveats: Figures 21 to 26 and Table 6 (context diagram, architecture domains, Zachman framework, enterprise data model layers, subject area models, data flow matrix and diagram) are missing from the converted text; no statement here rests on them.
The Context Agent exists only as a content-area list in ARCHITECTURE.md and docs/PROPOSED-ARCHITECTURE.md and has no contract, so the comparison is against intent, not a built artefact.

'Enterprise data products' is not a DMBOK2 term; the nearest passage describes data services offered inside an organisation, and treating them as equivalent is an interpretation for human confirmation.
rows.status_rationale: ARCHITECTURE.md lists enterprise data products and relevant source platforms as possible Context Agent content areas (docs/PROPOSED-ARCHITECTURE.md adds source-platform architecture to that agent's scope), which matches the DMBOK2 idea that stewardship needs architectural knowledge of systems and flows. The project does not say which architecture artefacts hold that knowledge, does not say whether a described platform or flow is current, planned or retired (its four evidence labels classify the statement, not the thing described), and leaves data flows to the Mapping & Lineage Agent, so the concept is present but misses elements the DMBOK2 asks for.
proposal_options: Add a three-value state qualifier (current, target, transition) to every Context Agent statement about a source platform or data flow, following the DMBOK2 practice of reflecting architecture specifications in current, target and transition state [DMBOK2-C04-03]; this is a small change to the evidence labels but relies on the organisation's architecture documents saying which state they describe [DMBOK2-C04-14].

Add an eight-value lifecycle status per source platform (Current, Deployment period, Strategic period, Retirement, Preferred, Containment, Emerging, Reviewed), following the DMBOK2 lifecycle projection categories [DMBOK2-C04-15] [DMBOK2-C04-16]; this is finer for platform planning but needs a maintained technology inventory that the project does not have.

additional_content.topic: Business rules harvesting and the four rule categories
additional_content.why_relevant: The DMBOK2 names data stewards among those who extract business rules from documentation and code and gives a four-way rule taxonomy, which bears on the evidence used by the Definition & CDE and Data Quality agents.

additional_content.topic: Profiling to test assumptions against actual data, balanced with privacy
additional_content.why_relevant: It supports the project rule that unsupported assumptions must be flagged and bears on the Mapping & Lineage Agent's open risk of reading production data values.

The DMBOK2 treats accuracy and completeness controls on data movement as part of integration design, which is where the evidence for an Exception & Root-Cause Agent about failed loads would originate.

additional_content.topic: Pairing a Data Steward with a data architect for each subject area
additional_content.why_relevant: It bears on the project's single-steward operating model, since the DMBOK2 pairs a steward with an architect at subject-area and entity level.

additional_content.topic: Interface sprawl, data copies and replication as sources of inconsistency
additional_content.why_relevant: It names concrete structural causes of inconsistent data that an Exception & Root-Cause Agent could test as hypotheses.

additional_content.topic: Event-triggered governance reviews and approval controls for integration changes
additional_content.why_relevant: It shows one way to map escalation triggers to governance reviews and approval gates, relevant to the project's escalation conditions and human-approval points.

source_caveats: Figures 21 to 27 and Table 6 in Chapter 4, and Figures 66 to 70 in Chapter 8, are missing from the converted text (their image links are dead), so the data flow matrix and diagram, enterprise data model layers, ETL and ELT flows, coupling diagram and architecture-domain table cannot be checked; no row relies on them except where its caveats say so.

The conversion drops some hyphens and bullet markers (for example 'twodimensional', 'eventdriven', 'bottomup'), merges neighbouring list items onto one line (for example the mapping-specification items on PDF page 490) and wraps some cross-references in underline tags, so list membership is inferred from context and quotes were chosen to avoid these artefacts.

Heading marks are inconsistent in the conversion (some numbered headings appear only as italic or bold text, and '1. Introduction' carries a full stop); the section field gives the nearest numbered heading above each quote with any trailing full stop removed.

Chapters 4 and 8 describe lineage, mapping, data sharing agreements and master data mainly as concerns for architects and integration teams and mention Data Steward roles only in passing, so statements about stewardship duties are inferred from where stewards are named.

The terms 'data contract' and 'enterprise data product' do not appear in this 2017-edition text; the data sharing agreement, data exchange specification and data services mappings used here are interpretations for human confirmation.

Chapters 5, 6, 7, 9, 12, 13 and 14 are cross-referenced from this range but lie outside it, and Chapter 10 (reference and master data) is read in unit 4; rows A-15, A-16, A-17, A-25 and A-26 rest on Chapters 4 and 8 only and should be merged with the units that read those chapters.
